subject: economics
objective: Given a news event about a market, say whether it shifts demand, shifts supply, or is only a change in the good's own price (a movement along a curve); say which way the curve shifts; predict the change in equilibrium price and quantity and explain it through the shortage or surplus at the old price; and predict whether a price ceiling or floor causes a shortage, a surplus, or no effect.
prerequisites: Reading a graph with two axes
candidateStandards: Oklahoma Academic Standards for Social Studies, high school Economics: price and non-price factors in supply and demand; shortages and surpluses including price ceilings and floors (verify current version and exact codes with the teacher)
Council for Economic Education, Voluntary National Content Standards in Economics, 2nd ed. (2010), Standard 7 (Markets and Prices) and Standard 8 (Role of Prices), grade 12 benchmarks
sources: OpenStax, Principles of Economics 3e, Chapter 3: Demand and Supply, Sections 3.1 to 3.5 (https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/3-4-price-ceilings-and-price-floors)

Council for Economic Education, Voluntary National Content Standards in Economics, 2nd ed. (2010), Standards 7 and 8 (https://www.councilforeconed.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/03/voluntary-national-content-standards-2010.pdf)
misconceptions: A change in a good's own price shifts its demand or supply curve (demand versus quantity demanded)
Whoever is affected by the news is the curve that shifts (a heat wave shifts ice cream supply)
A decrease in supply is a shift down
Supply increasing raises price, or demand changes move price and quantity in opposite directions
When both curves shift, both price and quantity can be predicted
Equilibrium means everyone gets the good, or that the price is fair
Any price ceiling causes a shortage, even one above equilibrium
A price ceiling lets more people buy the good
modelLimitations: The strawberry market is invented: straight-line curves Qd = 18,000 − 2,000P and Qs = 3,000P − 2,000 (boxes per week), one kind of box, and a price everyone can see.
Every shift in part 3 and in the practice sketches is 5,000 boxes so new prices are whole dollars; the double-shift sketch uses equal shifts and says so.
The price-adjust animation closes 30% of the gap per step; it shows the direction of pressure, not the speed of real adjustment.
Part 1 counts a buyer whose top price equals the price as buying, and a grower whose cost equals the price as selling.
Consumer surplus under a ceiling assumes scarce boxes go to the buyers who value them most.
Lines, black markets, and quality changes under price controls are described in text, not modeled.
Rent control and the minimum wage are named as examples only, with a note that real effects are studied and debated.
Strawberries are treated as a normal good; one practice headline uses an inferior good and says so.
